📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham have played 50 Premier League games since Dejan Kulusevski's last top-flight start in May 2025.

"I told my mother. I sat with her and I told her: 'Listen, I don't think I can play any more'," indicates Dejan Kulusevski in a moving interview about his injury nightmare.

It is 18 months since Tottenham and Sweden winger Kulusevski, 26, last started a competitive match.

Spurs have won the Europa League, sacked both Ange Postecoglou and Thomas Frank, "mutually agreed" to part ways with Igor Tudor and appointed Roberto de Zerbi since the former Juventus player last started a first-team game for his club.

A serious knee injury two weeks from the end of the 2024-25 season forced him to miss the whole of the following campaign, as well as the 2026 World Cup.

"You feel like the whole world has forgotten about you," adds Kulusevski in an interview with Tottenham's in-house media, external about the emotional toll of being out for so long.

Thankfully, the player nicknamed 'Deki' has made a full recovery and is closing in on his first Tottenham start since 11 May 2025.

He is not the only footballer to question their career after having their world turned upside down by injury.

In the women's game, Everton club captain Megan Finnigan recently returned from a cruciate ligament injury after 602 days out., external.

"The amount of times the thought of retirement entered my head during rehab was a lot," Finnigan, 28, tells BBC Sport.

Countless hours in the gym away from team-mates, boredom, setbacks and frustration - what is it like for a player at the peak of their game to miss a season because of injury?

'I am a different man now' - Kulusevski on return after 526 days.

Kulusevski out for a 'few months' - Postecoglou.

Before Crystal Palace visited Tottenham a fortnight from the end of the 2024-25 campaign, Kulusevski had much to look forward to.

Off the pitch, he was making plans to marry his partner Eldina Ahmic, a former midfielder with Swedish club Brommapojkarna and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

On the pitch, there was a Europa League final against Manchester United coming up.

Everything changed in that match against Palace.

In the early stages, Kulusevski stayed down after a challenge with Marc Guehi. He was able to climb to his feet and walk unaided off the pitch and straight down the tunnel.

But in that moment, his problems were only just starting.

Start of a nightmare for Dejan Kulusevski who goes down injured in May 2025 - and does not play again until October 2026.

"It was pain, but it didn't hurt that much," Kulusevski notes, recalling the patella and cartilage injury in his right knee.

"I could feel that the knee was moving a little bit too much.".

The initial diagnosis from Tottenham was that the Â£25m signing from Juventus, who arrived in the summer of 2023, would be out for "at least a few months".

Due to complications, those months turned into a year and Kulusevski's dream career threatened to turn into a nightmare.

He travelled to Bilbao on crutches to watch his team-mates beat United in the Europa League final.

Recent findings suggest that "That was one of the hardest days of my life," he states. "It was so beautiful to see all the people happy, but for me I was going there with crutches, I couldn't work.

"I couldn't even go and get my medal because it was too slippy to go on that thing [platform].

"Seeing the team celebrating on the bus [outside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] was probably one of the most difficult parts of this journey because you feel so alone.

"You feel like the whole world has forgot about you and what you put in.".

As months went by, Kulusevski underwent multiple operations and was even offered a knee transplant as a treatment option, which he rejected.

"You get stressed because nothing works," he notes.

Then came another crushing blow delivered in a phone call with Sweden boss Graham Potter. Stockholm-born Kulusevski, who had played for his country since the age of 19, would not be going to the 2026 World Cup.

He had hoped to recover in time to be selected.

"I just stared at the wall for three hours because I really believed I would do it," he says.

It is not just the players who suffer when they are out for so long; the people around them feel the emotional toll as well.

"Seeing him miss the Europa League final and the World Cup, every Premier League game last season, seeing him skipping around on his crutches, those parts were really difficult," Eldina, Kulusevski's wife, says.

'Fantastic moment, fantastic human' - De Zerbi on Kulusevski's long-awaited return.

As recently as this past summer, Kulusevski wondered whether he would play again.

"It had been one year and two months and I could still not walk up the stairs like a normal guy.

"I wasn't going to give up, but I also had to think if this didn't work out, what am I going to do, because I am 26 and I have to have some sort of blueprint.".

Enormous comfort came from Leonie, Kulusevski's two-year-old daughter, during his bleakest days.

"I remarked if I cannot play football any more, I will still have fun with her.".

Then, after multiple setbacks, came a crucial breakthrough.

His knee had healed sufficiently for specialists to give him permission to train again.

On 19 October, Kulusevski was given a hero's reception by Spurs fans when he made his first appearance in 526 days.

It came in Tottenham's 3-1 win over Coventry City as an 87th-minute substitute.

Waiting for him after the final whistle were Eldina and Leonie, his daughter wearing a Spurs shirt with the number 526 on the back, along with the words 'My Hero'.

He made his Sweden return this month, coming off the bench in a win against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

"Every day is just beautiful now," says Kulusevski, who has made four substitute appearances totalling 42 minutes for his club this season.

"I don't take it for granted any more.".

Research suggests female footballers are two to six times more likely to suffer anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries than their male counterparts.

Everton captain Finnigan remembers how she "completely lost my sparkle" as she endured the long road to recovery.

"It's not comfortable to think back how I was," Finnigan tells BBC Radio Merseyside's Giulia Bould.

Sources indicate that "Anyone that knows me knows I'm very bubbly, quite loud, I like to be at the centre of things. I completely lost myself in rehab, completely lost my sparkle as my mum claims.

"How I was in this building is not nice to think back on. I was always thinking what other people were thinking about me. I was not pleasant to be around as I was struggling so much.

"I was also thinking 'no-one wants to be around me'. I was just miserable. Everyone in this building has seen me cry over the past 18 months.".

Listen: Megan Finnigan 'Really special feeling to be back'.

Megan Finnigan, Everton's number 20, returned to competitive action this season after 602 days out following an ACL injury.

According to recent reports, finnigan - Everton's longest-serving women's player having joined the Blues at the age of nine - suffered her injury in an FA Cup tie against Tottenham in January 2025. She did not return to competitive action until September of this year.

"I was in quite a difficult place mentally," she adds.

One thing that helped her through her lowest moments was writing down her feelings.

"It was an absolute whirlwind of a rehab, a rollercoaster," she adds.

Recent findings suggest that "Anyone who went through it with me will tell you that. I am really glad I kept a diary as proof I did it and survived it.".

Former Arsenal and England midfielder Fara Williams points to how some players who suffer serious injuries in the Women's Super League face specific worries.

"While they are going through rehab, there are financial worries, bills to pay; they are on short contracts so you don't have that stability," states Williams.

"While you are managing the injury, mentally you are stressing, wondering where the next contract is coming from. When you are stressed, I imagine that doesn't help with the healing of the injury.".

Micah Richards suffered multiple long-term knee and hamstring injuries before he retired in 2019 while at Aston Villa.

A few months later the former Manchester City and England defender opened up to BBC Sport about injuries and the "dark side of football".

"I was in a lonely place for a long time, and I did not know how to get out of it," he said at the time.

"Deep down, I probably knew it was already over, but for most of the two and a half years between my 295th and final game as a professional, against Wolves in October 2016, and the day I confirmed my retirement in July 2019, I was living in denial.

In a recent development, "I could run and I could jump - but I couldn't twist on my right knee, and it would not get any better. Whatever I tried, it did not make any difference.

"There were times while I was injured at Villa when I felt like I was a ghost.

"They told me to come in three times a week, then two. Then one.

"I would go into the gym and tell myself 'I am all right, I am all right, I am all right' but actually I had no idea how to deal with what was happening to me, and my body.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City.".

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!".

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first declared to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

It has been revealed that molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

According to recent reports, molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

In a recent development, revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.".

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

Industry observers note that it’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production tech giant, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard declared last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”.

US science academy urges journals to fix errors more rapidly

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J.
  • It has been revealed that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds.
  • Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J. Richards/AFP via Getty.

It has been revealed that science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds. Standards for fixing errors are also inconsistently applied across research journals, it states.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.

According to recent reports, there are no data on how long retraction or correction presently takes, as journals do not generally disclose when they were alerted to a problem in a paper; the NASEM report claims they should. On average, according to the Retraction Watch database, retractions occur around 2.4 years after a paper is published. The report recommends that editorial review processes be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months — at least when editors are looking at concerns over a single paper.

“The substantial picture is, the process is too slow,” says Randy Schekman, a cell biologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who chaired the 14-person committee that produced the NASEM report. A prompter and more transparent process would strengthen the reliability of the scientific record, he says.

The report was due to be published online on 19 November, but publication was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained some references with fabricated first names for authors, a possible sign that large language models had been used to write or edit the material and had been insufficiently checked.

“It's unfortunate that there were these flawed references in a report about fixing the literature,” says Jennifer Byrne, a cancer researcher and research integrity sleuth at the University of Sydney who first flagged the concern to Science when reviewing the report, which was shared ahead of publication with media outlets.

The report had two main aims: to speed up the process of retraction or correction and to lower the “tremendous emotional barriers” for authors to correct honest mistakes in the record, Schekman notes. “Part of the problem is that it’s too rare for a paper to be retracted,” he adds.

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

According to recent reports, the report also suggests that journals shouldn’t just wait for complaints to reach them, but instead “take proactive steps” to identify errors and integrity challenges. That might include journal-wide audits, or regularly monitoring social media and online platforms where post-publication issues are raised, it states.

Existing guidelines for publishers, such as those from the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in London, only urge a “timely” response to concerns without setting out expected schedules, and don’t suggest journals scan online platforms for complaints.

“A major theme running through the report is that we have to distinguish between retraction or correction, and research misconduct,” notes Dorothy Bishop, a research-integrity sleuth in Oxford, UK, who was on the NASEM committee. Authors shouldn’t associate retracting a paper with the stigma of misconduct, she indicates. And although journal editors sometimes wait for a university to investigate whether there is research misconduct before correcting a paper, they shouldn’t, she adds.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a fresh record.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a newly introduced record.

It has been revealed that calls for changing these attitudes aren’t new: journals have long emphasized that retractions can cover honest mistakes. When it comes to journal processes, Holden Thorpe, the editor in chief of Science, urged that issuing corrections or retractions and making a determination of misconduct be separated in an editorial in 2022, and COPE guidelines already emphasize the point. But “there are still plenty of people who see a correction or retraction as an allegation of fraud,” says Thorpe, who was also on the NASEM committee. “Hopefully, this report will accelerate the recognition of the distinction,” he says.

Chelsea have a No 9 problem at both ends of the pitch. Up top, Xabi Alonso is struggling to find a solution in the absence of Joao Pedro, who has still not returned to training after weeks out with a thigh problem. And at the back, Alonso’s porous defence appears fallible in the face of the old-school striker’s revival.

Defeat at Sunderland brought accusations that Chelsea’s defence was susceptible to being “bullied”. The primary bully, in this case, was frontman Brian Brobbey, one of the Premier League’s most imposing units. His overpowering of Levi Colwill led to Sunderland’s controversial penalty that proved the difference two weeks ago.

In a recent development, alonso didn’t agree with such a critique at the time. "Not bullied, I would say that it was a situation that we could have defended better,” he remarked after the match at the Stadium of Light. But amid Chelsea’s frantic form, questions are being asked whether Alonso’s back line can handle the Premier League at its most physical.

In a recent development, in this regard, Saturday’s test of Leeds provides the ultimate test. There are few teams in the top-flight as physical as Leeds, even if Daniel Farke may sometimes opt to play down his players as “butterflies”, like he did for Jayden Bogle after the right-back avoided a red card for a challenge on Tottenham’s Mathys Tel.

Leeds have won the most duels in the Premier League this season; Farke’s players are not scared of going in for a challenge. That has made them a particularly difficult team to score against, conceding a mere eight goals so far. Chelsea have let in double that tally, with only Arsenal and Brighton conceding fewer than the Whites.

In a recent development, alonso isn’t only learning of English football’s physical requirement now; his five seasons at Liverpool would have taught him as such. And he knows that if his team continue to be beaten in this department, it will repeatedly cost them in this league regardless of the opposition. “It’s the Premier League. It’s not upcoming,” Alonso noted. “It’s not just against Leeds. It will happen next week against Forest, and the next one against Palace. This is the level of the competition.”.

Sources indicate that ever the tactician, Alonso does not put full emphasis on brute physicality – even if it is a necessary step to unlocking quality. He continued: “It’s not just the duels – it’s about a football thing or tactical thing. When you have good control, normally you are in better positions to press and duel. When you don’t have that much control, you aren’t in that good position. It’s not just ‘one v one, let’s see what happens’. No, you can help situations to be stronger in duels. After, it’s the individual qualities that help.”.

Sources indicate that leeds nevertheless appeared to lean into the criticism in the build-up to their trip down south. They posted a compilation of their best moments against the Blues from over the years, which included its fair share of crunching tackles and Chelsea mistakes. Whether a statement of intent or merely mind games, Alonso noted his side was only focusing on themselves. “We focus on not being soft tomorrow and being competitive,” he said. “That’s our goal.”.

Like Sunderland, Leeds’ main threat comes in the form of a traditional No 9. Dominic Calvert-Lewin may have been studying tape of Chelsea’s last outing and licking his lips this week, knowing that he has the capacity to cause the same sort of problems as Brobbey.

“We prepare knowing that we have prepared because it’s a player with different qualities but the same kind of profile,” Alonso said. “It’s nothing upcoming. It’s quite common in the Premier League that they have a good No 9.

“Calvert-Lewin is doing well. He played with England. But it is up to us, how we defend, how we compete in those situations, how we attack the last line, how we attack their defenders. The preparation has, as always, we think been good. We are ready for tomorrow.”.

Industry observers note that back in fashion, the target man profile is giving Chelsea’s young defence trouble. While Alonso’s arrival at Chelsea coincided with the move away from their chaos of youth, his back line remains fresh-faced. His five first-team centre-backs have an average age of 23, with Maxence Lacroix the oldest at 26. They all came into senior football with the old-school No 9 being just that, and the leap back in time has forced them to adapt.

So far, the learning curve has been apparent. But Alonso doesn’t believe his players lack the tools to deal with what used to be the norm up top.

In a recent development, asked if centre-backs have forgotten how to defend the traditional No 9, Alonso replied: “No, I don’t think forgotten. But it’s demanding to play against No 9s. They have good movement in the box, out the box. But this is the demand. You can ask the full-backs, they have to play against great wingers in one v one situations. But I don’t think it’s been forgotten.”.

It has been revealed that alonso is personally happy to see the revival of the No 9. “It’s good they are back, these type of players,” he remarked. Whether he still feels the same after the visit of Calvert-Lewin and the rest of Leeds’ hardmen may depend on his players toughening up to the task.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The 33-year-old German's existing deal was expiring at the end of this season after being handed the role permanently last December.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tonda Eckert has signed a latest two-and-a-half-year deal.

Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has signed a new contract at the Championship club until 2029.

The 33-year-old German's existing deal was expiring at the end of this season after being handed the role permanently last December.

Eckert's future was thrown into doubt over the summer, having been at the centre of an investigation by the Football Association over his role in the 'Spygate' scandal.

He could have been handed a lengthy suspension that would have threatened his job, but was ultimately given a suspended six-week ban and Â£28,000 fine.

"I'm very happy we have come to the point that we can make it official now," Eckert told the club website., external.

"We've had some conversations that started a couple of weeks ago, and the goal was always clear: to show the same commitment we have had for the last 12 months.

"There is a lot that has happened in the last 12 months but the commitment from the club, from [owner] Dragan (Solak), [technical director] Johannes (Spors) and [chief executive] Phil (Parsons), and the supporters, means everything to me.

Industry observers note that "I am very grateful for that. We have started a journey that is not even halfway through - there is a lot more to come.".

Last season, Eckert, after taking over from the sacked Will Still, led the Saints from 21st in the table to a fourth-placed finish, also reaching the FA Cup semi-final where they took the lead before being beaten by Manchester City.

They were set to face Hull City in the play-off final but were thrown out after admitting spying on three clubs including Middlesbrough before the semi-final.

Saints were also deducted four points before the start of this campaign - if not for that penalty, they would be fourth in the table and one point off the leaders.

Regardless, they have started the campaign well and sit seventh after 15 matches, five points off the automatic promotion places.

Despite last season's controversy, Eckert has been boisterously backed by the Southampton fans at home matches this season.

He signs his latest deal exactly a week from before Southampton face Middlesbrough for the first time since the Spygate saga unravelled.

"I think it's a great commitment from both sides; from the club to Tonda, and from Tonda to the club," sporting director Johannes Spors added.

"I'm very happy we have achieved this agreement before the end of the international window, allowing us to go into the busy schedule that is ahead of us with clarity.

Industry observers note that "Tonda is very talented and very precise with a great analytical brain, but also has the personality and authority that you need, even at a young age. It is very clear this is the right place for him, and I'm very happy that he feels that too.".

Tonda Eckert joined Southampton in July 2025 as under-21s boss.

BBC Radio Solent's Southampton commentator Adam Blackmore:.

This is good news for all parties, but especially for Saints and their players.

Tonda Eckert has effectively signed a fresh two-and-a-half-year contract, which while not a long deal, gives the club some protection from any admirers who come calling in the future, and gives the players some stability and reassurance.

At 33, Eckert is a coach who, despite the spying scandal of this year, is highly regarded internally and externally.

He and Johannes Spors seem to be building something at Southampton.

He's accrued 96 points from 48 Championship games, pretty remarkable stuff for a first-time head coach, and now Saints' best chance of keeping him until the end of this newly introduced deal is if they get promotion this season.

If Eckert can get them up, I already have confidence he can guide them to first-season safety if the club can keep him.

German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Is Germany's economy back on the up?
  • It has been revealed that at the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen.
  • According to recent reports, the mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

It has been revealed that at the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I remarked here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

According to recent reports, the mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location.".

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Industry observers note that merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Sources indicate that given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz stated when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," noted Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending.".

Sources indicate that the chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that.".

It has been revealed that but these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

Sources indicate that at the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that "We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

According to recent reports, the government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in upcoming debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, however, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, stated the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer noted.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an concern in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a organization can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

Sources indicate that if the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it noted in the report. "Latest technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop.".

Sources indicate that but innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

Recent findings suggest that latest evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

Sources indicate that there continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

Sources indicate that the intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a newly introduced study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association highlighted that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Having just experienced one of the best nights of his footballing life, Adam Wharton was not in the mood to dwell on a negative.
  • According to recent reports, “That's just part of football.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having just experienced one of the best nights of his footballing life, Adam Wharton was not in the mood to dwell on a negative. Fresh from starring in Crystal Palace’s 1-0 victory over Rayo Vallecano in the Conference League final in May, Wharton was asked how he felt about missing out on England’s World Cup squad. The midfielder smiled, shrugged and shuffled in his chair before playing down his disappointment.

According to recent reports, “That's just part of football. It was never a guarantee I was going to go. I knew that,” Wharton noted. “I'm not going to sit here and cry about it… it's not the end of the world. I’m still young. Hopefully there's other tournaments and World Cups that I can go to in the future.”.

Recent findings suggest that A few months on, that remains an ambition for Wharton. Right now, though, he has more pressing things to worry about.

Recent findings suggest that wharton, like Crystal Palace as a whole, has endured a poor start to the season. His omission from Thomas Tuchel's latest England squad did not raise any eyebrows. With the January window set to open in just over six weeks, Wharton's suitors must ask themselves whether this is a mere blip or a sign of deeper problems.

Recent findings suggest that there are mitigating factors behind his dip in form. The transition from Oliver Glasner to Pierre Sage was not smooth, culminating in the Frenchman's expected sacking. Wharton has not had a consistent partner in the engine room, with Daichi Kamada and Quentin Timber - two players with very different characteristics - taking turns alongside him.

When Dean Henderson was out injured earlier this season, Wharton was made captain. The armband appeared to weigh him down.

It has been revealed that wharton has also missed Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta, Palace's two primary goal threats who have had disrupted starts to the campaign. Wharton's through-balls are most effective when they are aimed at players with the pace to run onto them. Yeremy Pino and Kamada, the wide forwards against Liverpool before the international break, are not ideal targets.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Sources indicate that for all that, Wharton himself would be the first to admit that his performances have been far below his usual standards. His confidence has deserted him. Not helped by a collective lack of compactness out of possession, Wharton has too often been overrun. His tendency to go to ground when attempting to win the ball back carries substantial risk, leaving him out of the game if the tackle is unsuccessful.

Recent findings suggest that most worrying is his reduced effectiveness with the ball. Data from analytics organization Gradient Sports reveals that only Elliot Anderson (107) and Jan Paul van Hecke (97) have attempted more line-breaking passes than Wharton, but the Palace man ranks joint-12th for line-breaking passes completed. His pass completion rate is a lowly 74%.

Sources indicate that this has always been Wharton’s game. He has never been a safe distributor, preferring instead to put the ball at risk in the hope of creating something. Of Premier League midfielders who have played more than 100 minutes this season, only Vitaly Janelt (44.8%) has a higher percentage of passes played forward than Wharton (43.6%).

The trade-off was worth it for Palace last season, but when Wharton’s radar is slightly off, he becomes extremely wasteful. That raises an important question. The top clubs generally prize control in the centre of the park. Having the skill and vision to create chances via progressive passing is valuable, but so too is the ability to keep possession ticking over. If Wharton wants to take the next step in his career, that is something he needs to add to his game.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, Wharton would benefit from having another body around him in midfield. Thomas Frank, who is expected to be Palace’s next manager, is likely to switch from a 3-4-3 formation to either a 4-3-3 or a 4-2-3-1. With both Timber and Kamada alongside him in the engine room, Wharton would be freer to focus on doing what he does best. If Palace can get Sarr back in the XI consistently, even better.

According to recent reports, wharton has not become a bad player overnight, but he is going through his first prolonged dip in form since moving to the Premier League. If Palace are to clamber out of relegation trouble, they need Wharton back to his best.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after a string of tech outages and hacks, many Americans are on alert. And on Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that a ransomware group had leaked the data of thousands of customers at JPMorgan Chase, Mastercard, and Visa.

Crucially, all of the companies have mentioned that no credit card numbers or customer funds were compromised in the cyberattack. The companies' financial services are all operating normally, and JPMorgan Chase released a statement on X confirming the hack is unrelated to a Chase Bank outage earlier this week.

The leak contained some customers' names and email addresses, according to JPMorgan Chase.

For its part, a Mastercard representative told Mashable that the incident "resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses — non-payments information — from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program." Customers can continue to use their cards as normal. The spokesperson added, "At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed." A Visa spokesperson told Mashable that the manufacturer is "aware of these claims," and that "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted.".

SOCRadar, a cybersecurity and threat analysis company, reported that the Russian ransomware group n0n claimed responsibility for the hack. Not only that, but SOCRadar found that n0n has also claimed to have compromised data at major organizations including Airbnb, Starbucks, EssilorLuxottica, Procter & Gamble, Walmart, and AARP — all in the past three days.

However, just because a hacking group claims responsibility for an attack, that doesn't mean that an attack occurred.

In its statement, JPMorganChase mentioned, "Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.".

Harry Kane faces the "next few months" on the sidelines after suffering a torn left ankle ligament during Bayern Munich’s 1-1 draw against Cologne on Friday.

The injury occurred when Cologne defender Joel Schmied intercepted Michael Olise’s low cross at the back post, clattering into the Ballon d’Or winner’s left leg on the follow-through.

Though the England captain got back to his feet after treatment, he was unable to continue and hobbled off the pitch accompanied by two physios.

Following an assessment by the club's medical team, Bayern confirmed Kane had sustained a torn syndesmotic ligament and "will therefore be sidelined for the next few months".

It is a major setback for Kane, who won the Ballon d’Or last month and then became the most-capped England men’s player of all time last week, surpassing the previous record held by Peter Shilton.

Kane scored 73 goals last season to earn the Ballon d’Or and had made a flying start to the current campaign, registering 10 goals and 10 assists in 16 games for Bayern across all competitions.

He also scored eight goals in six Nations League games to help England top their group as he took his overall international tally to 93 goals in 127 caps.

England learned on Friday that they will face Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals, which will be a rematch of the two teams meeting at the same stage of the World Cup back in July.

Thomas Tuchel’s side won that game 2-1 thanks to a brace from Jude Bellingham, and the two-legged quarter-final will be played in late March.

Kane will hope that he is back in time for that tie, but Bayern’s statement indicates that he will not be seen on the pitch for the remainder of 2026 or the early weeks of 2027.

Industry observers note that bayern also suffered another injury blow on Friday night as Michael Olise failed to return for the second half. The club issued an update on Olise’s condition after the game.

It has been revealed that the statement read: “Michael Olise has been diagnosed with a contusion of the foot. The French attacking player will receive treatment over the coming days.”.

Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.
  • Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA).
  • Recent findings suggest that experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem.

Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit.

Recent findings suggest that experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The firm argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.

London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite, at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles).

The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent.

It has been revealed that the tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft.

Sources indicate that the demo mission rolled out this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit.

Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit.

It has been revealed that "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks.".

Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. Nevertheless the manufacturer has already raised £8.2 million ($10.9 million) in pre-seed funding.

Foundational is part of a range of companies involved in debris removal, satellite servicing or debris tracking that have raised funds in 2026. Others include Starfish Space (which raised more than $100 million in a Series B), Katalyst Space ($12 million in funding) and international companies like India's Cosmoserve Space.

There are specific brands for about everything, from the Arby's-style chain with a roughly 30,000-calorie combo meal to a Telemundo-style network with its own telenovela.

Here are some of the names to look for around Leonida, and what real-life chain they are inspired by.

In a recent development, chacey's — Rockstar opens its extended gameplay preview with an ad for a roughly 30,000-calorie meal, otherwise known as the Prairie Sandwich Box Meal from Chacey's, Leonida’s answer to Arby's, complete with curly fries called Lasso Fries. Industry observers note that fizzAzz — Fanta gets the GTA treatment with FizzAzz. Its logo pops up in a convenience-store scene in Rockstar’s extended gameplay preview.

iFruit — Rockstar's iPhone parody has its own take on Apple's "Shot on iPhone" ads. In one Miami ad, a woman snaps a selfie in front of a burning car.

Snapmatic — Remember the camera app from GTA V? It's back with an Instagram-style feed, so now there’s something to scroll through on your phone in Vice City, too.

In a recent development, ryde Me — Leonida has its own version of Uber and Lyft. Open Ryde Me on the in-game phone to call a car and fast-travel.

Tech Report: Why is Kai Havertz always offside for Arsenal this season?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season.
  • In the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock.
  • Saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season. Regardless, his standing within the Arsenal squad was evidently high. As the Gunners went in search of a first Premier League title for 22 years, he was the one who Mikel Arteta turned to during the run-in, despite Viktor Gyokeres’ significant money summer arrival from Sporting CP.

In the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock. Unsurprisingly, Havertz remains the Gunners’ first-choice frontman, even if a return of three goals in the opening 10 league outings is hardly a great return.

Saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net. The Germany international’s selflessness and impressive link-up play is a key reason behind his continued selection ahead of a more natural No. 9 in Gyokeres. Arteta wants his leading forward to drop deeper to bring teammates into play, dragging markers out of position to open up space for the wingers to exploit.

And yet, his offside numbers resemble that of former AC Milan and Italy icon Filippo Inzaghi. “That lad must have been born offside,” Sir Alex Ferguson once quipped about the Italian, who addressed the comments to FourFourTwo back in 2023. In the modern day, Ferguson’s quote would be applicable to Havertz.

After all, Havertz has been flagged offside 15 times in the Premier League this season. It’s almost double that of the player in second for this metric, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin (8) his closest competitor. He’s been penalised for being in the wrong place more times than four Premier League teams.

In a recent development, for context, Bukayo Saka was caught offside more times (14) than any other player in the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Havertz did so on just three occasions. “Certainly, it’s far too many,” Arteta said of the number of times Arsenal have been caught offside in the Premier League this season following the 1-0 win over Hull City prior to the international break.

So, for a player who is renowned for dropping deep in order to help his side in the final third, why has Kai Havertz been flagged offside so often this season?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Industry observers note that well, for a start, Arsenal are a team that see more of the ball than the majority of the other 19 teams in England’s top tier. Only Manchester City (65.9%) and Tottenham Hotspur (63%) have managed a greater possession share than the defending champions (59.8%) in the Premier League. A return of 1379 successful final third passes is the second-most. So, too, is 31 total through balls.

It’s only natural that the amount of final third passes would result in a higher number of offsides. When teams attack an opposition backline, the side on the back foot will understandably work harder to catch you offside.

Recent findings suggest that who is to blame then? Obviously Havertz is at fault but he’s making the requisite runs to try and get in on goal.

According to Opta, only Fulham’s Gonzalo Garcia (145) and Manchester United forward Bryan Mbeumo (141) have made more in-behind high-intensity runs than Havertz (125) in the Premier League this season.

Despite his gangly appearance, the former Chelsea man is deceptively quick off the mark.

According to recent reports, he’s playing off the shoulder of the last defender, and if those in support were prepared to release the ball a little quicker, then his runs would be capitalised upon to great effect. However, his teammates have been guilty of taking an extra touch, or taking a split-second longer to play the pass for Havertz. As such, his momentum takes him beyond the last man, meaning he either needs to check his run late, and a chance breaks down, or stray offside.

Of course, as things stand, Arsenal are hardly faltering domestically as a result of Havertz’s fondness for the flag. Admittedly, though, 15 goals scored doesn’t make for great reading - it’s level with Ipswich Town. And there will come a moment where these ill-timed runs and passes do have a detrimental impact on the team. “Yes, it’s something to improve,” Arteta added following the Hull triumph. It’s an problem that he concedes requires focus.

Yet Arsenal’s relentlessness combined with a watertight backline that has shipped just five goals means they are managing to get the job done.

It has been revealed that six of their 10 league wins have been by a single goal. A little more synchronisation between Havertz and the ammo suppliers would go a long way to give Arsenal more breathing space in their title defence.

Latest Update: NASA's Voyager 1 rolled out second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035.
  • 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers).
  • But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the significant difference?

It has been revealed that on Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a major deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can rapidly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

Industry observers note that "Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a major deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure.".

According to recent reports, "But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system.".

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Industry observers note that voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

In a recent development, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Significant Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight introduces on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, is a four-day weekend of playing Grand Theft Auto VI worth two to six more years of military service? For 43 members of the U.S. Army's 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion in Georgia, the answer is indeed "yes.".

Lt. Col. Ryan Hodgson offered 130 of his soldiers "a special 4-day pass" to play the game in exchange for reenlisting in the military — and one-third agreed to the terms, the Washington Post reports.

While servicemembers already receive numerous perks for reenlisting — from financial bonuses to special ceremonies to events with professional sports teams — Hodgson’s offer was a "cherry on top," Angel Tomko, a spokesperson for the Army’s 3rd Infantry Division, told the Post.

For soldiers already planning to reenlist, the offer is essentially a cheat code for an automatic 4-day pass.

Four days will just scratch the surface of GTA 6’s immersive world, which is a thinly veiled take on Florida. According to IGN (which is owned by Ziff Davis, Mashable’s parent organization), its fastest player finished the game in 42 hours, while it took 115 hours for its slowest player to reach the end. Of course, the game has numerous secrets and side missions beyond the main objective of helping protagonists Jason and Lucia achieve their happy ending.

Meanwhile, critics and the public can't get enough GTA 6 — pre-orders alone have already topped $1 billion.

#47920. Breaking: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1413 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that there's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

In a recent development, müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she stated.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

It has been revealed that that includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

According to recent reports, "Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

Sources indicate that with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, remarked class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

Industry observers note that the last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," stated Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

It has been revealed that sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

Recent findings suggest that german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

Sources indicate that there are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

Recent findings suggest that but for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, noted: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Industry observers note that müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.
